stage_2_story.text_en:
Last Tuesday, David woke up feeling unwell. His main symptoms were a sore throat, a headache, and a mild fever of thirty-eight degrees. He decided to call his family doctor and make an appointment for the same morning.

When David arrived at the clinic, he checked in at the front desk and sat down in the waiting room. There were a few other patients ahead of him, so he waited about fifteen minutes before the nurse called his name.

The doctor examined David carefully. She looked at his throat, listened to his chest, and measured his temperature again. After the examination, her diagnosis was a bacterial throat infection. She explained the treatment clearly — a five-day course of antibiotics — and wrote a prescription that David could take to any pharmacy.

David asked if he needed to see a specialist. The doctor said it was not necessary for now, but if the symptoms did not improve after a week, she would refer him to one. She also reminded him to book his annual checkup soon. David thanked her, picked up the prescription, and stopped at the pharmacy on his way home. By the next morning, he already felt a little better.
